chapter_summary:
An array is a collection of values of the same type stored under one name. Arrays are useful when you need to store multiple related values, such as a history of sensor readings or a sequence of LED pins. You declare an array by specifying the type, name, and size:

```cpp
int ledPins[] = {3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11};
```

In this example, the compiler automatically determines the size based on the number of values. You access individual elements using an index, starting from 0:

```cpp
ledPins[0] = 255;  // sets the first element
```

A common pattern is to iterate over an array with a `for` loop:

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
  pinMode(ledPins[i], OUTPUT);
}
```

This loop configures each pin in the array as an output. Arrays make it easy to manage groups of related hardware pins without writing repetitive code.

Strings in Arduino can be represented in two ways. A C-string is an array of characters ending with a special null character `\0`. C-strings are memory-efficient but can be tricky to manipulate. The Arduino `String` class is easier to use but dynamically allocates memory, which can lead to memory fragmentation and program crashes on microcontrollers with limited RAM. For small, fixed messages, C-strings are preferred. For complex text processing, the `String` class may be acceptable on boards with more memory.

Memory on the Arduino Uno is limited. SRAM, which holds variables while the program runs, is only 2 KB. Flash memory, which stores the program, is 32 KB. EEPROM is 1 KB and is used for non-volatile storage. Because SRAM is small, you should avoid large arrays, long strings, and excessive use of the `String` class. The `F()` macro helps save RAM by keeping constant strings in flash memory:

```cpp
Serial.println(F("This message stays in flash memory"));
```

Understanding memory constraints is a key part of embedded programming. As your projects grow, you will need to balance functionality with the limited resources of the microcontroller.

screens.title: Arrays, Strings, and Memory Basics
screens.subtitle: Manage collections, text, and limited RAM on small Arduino boards

narration.text: In this lesson we will learn how arrays gather related values under one name, how different kinds of strings behave on Arduino, and why memory types matter on small microcontrollers. You will see concrete code patterns for declaring and indexing arrays, a straightforward lab for computing averages and finding extremes, and a careful comparison between C-style character arrays and the Arduino String object. We will also explore the three storage areas on a board — flash, SRAM, and EEPROM — and a simple trick to keep constant text out of scarce R A M. These ideas matter because even simple projects can crash if they exhaust small amounts of SRAM. For a quick example, you will learn a loop pattern that configures several pins from one array, and a practice step that computes the average of five sensor readings. By the end you will understand how to choose the right text representation and how to size arrays so your sketch stays reliable. Think about a small data buffer in SRAM: what could happen if you keep growing it without control?

screens.title: What is an Array?
screens.subtitle: A typed collection with contiguous indexed elements

narration.text: An array is a fixed collection of values that all share the same type and are stored under one name. Think of it as a row of labeled boxes where each box holds a single item and is reached by a numeric index that starts at zero. You declare arrays by giving a type, a name, and either an explicit size or an initializer list. For example, a list of LED pins can be written so the compiler infers the number of entries from the initial values. This saves you from counting sizes manually and keeps declarations concise. When you access elements, use the zero-based index to read or assign a value; an off-by-one or an index equal to the array size will reference memory outside the array and cause undefined behavior. A common misconception is that arrays automatically resize; they do not. On microcontrollers arrays are static unless you implement your own dynamic allocation. A practical example is keeping the pin numbers for a string of LEDs in one array so you can configure or write to each pin in a simple loop. Key takeaway: arrays group related values, but you must manage bounds and lifetime explicitly.

keyIdea.title: Array definition
keyIdea.text: A fixed-size, typed collection accessed by zero-based indexes; does not auto-resize.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › What is an Array?
Definition

Typed collection with indexed elements

Arrays store values of the same type in contiguous memory slots. Each slot is accessed with a zero-based index. They are ideal for lists such as pin numbers or a short history of sensor readings.

Example Declaration
int ledPins[] = {3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11};
ledPins[0] = 255;  // set first element
Common Mistake
Assuming arrays auto-resize. They are fixed unless you use dynamic allocation, which is discouraged on small microcontrollers.
Key Takeaway
Use arrays to reduce repetitive code and keep related values together. Always check bounds.

Out-of-bounds access reads or writes memory outside the array and can crash the program. Confirm loop bounds carefully.

screens.title: Iterating Arrays with for Loops
screens.subtitle: A reliable loop pattern for configuring pins and processing readings

narration.text: Iterating an array with a for loop is a core pattern in Arduino sketches. The loop sets up a simple integer index that starts at zero and advances while it is less than the array size. This avoids off-by-one errors when you use the array length in the condition. A practical microcontroller example is configuring a list of LED pins as outputs. You declare the array of pin numbers, then run a for loop that calls the pin configuration function for each element. Another common use is processing sensor values: you sum each entry and then compute an average by dividing by the count. Important details include choosing the correct loop limit — use the number of elements directly — and using an index variable type that matches your platform. A misconception is to use less-than-or-equal-to with a zero-based index, which leads to a boundary error. In a code walkthrough you will see initializing accumulators, updating min and max inside the same loop, and ensuring the initial min and max values make sense for your sensor range. A quick check after the loop guards against divide-by-zero when the array size could be zero.

keyIdea.title: Loop pattern
keyIdea.text: Use for loops with a zero-based index and strict less-than limit to traverse arrays safely.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Iterating Arrays
Pattern

for loop traversal

Use an index starting at zero and loop while it is less than the number of elements. This pattern works both for configuring pins and for aggregating sensor values.

Configuration Example
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
  pinMode(ledPins[i], OUTPUT);
}
Pro Tip
When counting elements, prefer constants or computed sizes so loops remain correct when the array changes.
Common Mistake
Using i <= size uses one index past the array end. Always use less-than with zero-based arrays.
Walkthrough
Summing readings and tracking min and max in one pass keeps code efficient and easy to test.
What to initialize
  • Set an accumulator to zero before the loop.
  • Initialize min to a very large value or the first element.
  • Initialize max to a very small value or the first element.
Example Scenario
A loop that reads five sensor values can compute sum, mean, min and max in one pass, minimizing SRAM and CPU time.

screens.title: Average, Minimum, and Maximum — Lab Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step code to compute average and find extremes in a sensor array

narration.text: Let's walk through a simple lab: start with an array of five integer readings, compute the average, and then extend the code to find the highest and lowest readings. Begin by declaring the array and assigning example values. Next, initialize an accumulator to zero. Use a for loop with an index from zero to the array length minus one. Inside the loop add each element to the accumulator. After the loop, divide the accumulator by the number of readings to find the mean; decide whether to use integer or floating-point division depending on required precision. To find min and max without a second pass, initialize both to the first array element before the loop or set min to a very large sentinel and max to a very small sentinel, then update them when a new smaller or larger value appears. A common trap is initializing min to zero when all readings are positive; that will never update correctly. After coding, test with known inputs to verify results. This lab maps directly to hands-on practice: you will write the loop, test with sample numbers, and observe correct averages and extremes.

keyIdea.title: Lab focus
keyIdea.text: One-pass loop can compute sum, average, min, and max efficiently; initialize correctly and test with sample data.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Average & Min/Max Walkthrough
Starter Code
int readings[5] = {100, 102, 98, 105, 101};
int sum = 0;
int minVal = readings[0];
int maxVal = readings[0];
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  int v = readings[i];
  sum += v;
  if (v < minVal) minVal = v;
  if (v > maxVal) maxVal = v;
}
float average = sum / 5.0;
This code computes sum, updates min and max, and then computes a floating-point average to avoid truncation.
Checks & Pitfalls
  • Confirm the array length in the loop condition matches the declared size.
  • Initialize min and max sensibly; using the first element is often simplest.
  • Decide integer versus float division for average to match precision needs.
  • Test with edge cases: identical values, increasing or decreasing sequences.
Try This
Modify the code to ignore sensor readings below a threshold and recompute average only for valid samples.

screens.title: C-strings: Character Arrays and the Null Terminator
screens.subtitle: Memory-efficient text using character arrays ending with a terminator

narration.text: C-style strings are arrays of characters that end with a special null terminator. In practice you allocate a character array with enough slots for the visible characters plus the null. This representation is memory-efficient because it keeps the characters in a single contiguous block and avoids dynamic allocation. It is also low-level: you must manage sizes, copying, and concatenation carefully to prevent overflow. One helpful example is storing a short message in a fixed character array for printing to the serial console. A common misconception is that the terminator is optional; without it string-handling functions will continue reading memory until they find a zero value, producing garbage or crashes. Compared with the Arduino String class, C-strings trade convenience for predictability and lower SRAM usage. When your messages are short and fixed, C-strings are the safer choice on boards with small SRAM. Always reserve one extra character for the terminator and test operations that copy or join strings to avoid overruns. C-strings: Character Arrays and the Null Terminator means character array plus a null terminator; low memory overhead but requires careful size management.. In practical terms, memory-efficient text using character arrays ending with a terminator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: C-string core
keyIdea.text: Character array plus a null terminator; low memory overhead but requires careful size management.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › C-strings
Definition

Character arrays with terminator

C-strings are arrays holding characters plus a null terminator at the end. They avoid runtime allocation and are predictable in memory use, making them preferred for small fixed messages.

Practical note
Always leave one extra slot for the terminator when declaring buffers and check lengths before copying or concatenating strings.
Concrete Example
Store a small message for repeated Serial prints without using heap memory. This keeps SRAM usage low and predictable.
Misconception Check
Don't assume C functions will guard your buffers. Always ensure destination size is sufficient before copying characters.
Key Takeaway
Use C-strings for small fixed messages to avoid dynamic memory overhead and fragmentation.

screens.title: C-strings vs. Arduino String Object
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs between memory efficiency and convenience

narration.text: There are two common ways to use text on Arduino: C-style character arrays and the Arduino String object. C-strings are arrays ending in a null terminator. They keep memory usage predictable because their size is fixed and allocated in static or stack memory. The Arduino String class is easier to manipulate with concatenation and length queries, but it performs dynamic memory allocation on the heap. On boards with very limited SRAM, like many classic Arduino models, repeated String operations can fragment the heap and eventually cause allocation failures and program crashes. That is the main practical trade-off: convenience versus long-term reliability. If you need to do simple, fixed prints, prefer C-strings. If your board has abundant R A M or you need lots of text processing, String may be acceptable. A useful habit is to profile memory usage early in development and to favor C-strings for constant messages while restricting String usage to parts of the code where convenience outweighs the risk. A misconception is thinking String is always safe on small boards; it is not. End with this reflection: which text pattern will keep your sketch running reliably when memory is tight?

keyIdea.title: Comparison summary
keyIdea.text: C-strings are memory-predictable; String objects are convenient but can fragment SRAM on low-memory boards.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › C-strings vs String
C-strings
Fixed-size character arrays with a terminator. Low SRAM use and predictable allocation. Best for short constant messages and tight memory budgets.
Pros
  • Predictable memory usage
  • No heap fragmentation
  • Good for constant or short messages
Arduino String
A higher-level class that makes text manipulation easier by allocating memory on demand. Convenient but risky on low-RAM boards due to fragmentation over time.
Cons
  • Dynamic allocation can fragment SRAM
  • Not recommended for repeated small boards or long-running sketches with many allocations
Guideline
Prefer C-strings for fixed messages. Use String only when board memory and lifetime behavior are acceptable.

screens.title: Memory on Arduino: Flash, SRAM, and EEPROM
screens.subtitle: Understand the three storage areas and their purposes

narration.text: Arduino boards have three distinct storage areas with different roles. Flash stores the compiled program and constant data; it is large relative to SRAM and is read-only while the sketch runs. SRAM is the board's working memory: it holds variables, arrays, and dynamic allocations while the program executes. On many classic boards SRAM is small — measured in kilobytes — so it fills quickly if you keep large arrays or many dynamic strings. EEPROM provides a small persistent area for non-volatile data that survives power cycles; it is useful for saving calibration values or small configuration items. For example, a typical Uno-like board might have tens of kilobytes of flash, a couple of kilobytes of SRAM, and a kilobyte of EEPROM. The practical implications are straightforward: keep large constant text in flash, keep runtime buffers small, and reserve EEPROM for only tiny persistent records. The F macro is an easy tool to keep serial print constants in flash instead of copying them into SRAM. A misconception is believing all memory is interchangeable — it is not. Pick the right room for each kind of data to avoid running out of working memory during runtime.

keyIdea.title: Memory roles
keyIdea.text: Flash holds code and constants, SRAM is the working memory for variables, EEPROM stores small persistent data across power cycles.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Memory on Arduino
Flash
Holds the program and constant data. Large relative to SRAM and read-only at runtime. Use for constant strings and code.
SRAM
Working memory for variables, arrays, and dynamic allocations. Very limited on many boards; avoid large buffers.
EEPROM
Small persistent storage for calibration or configuration that must survive power cycles.
Practical Sizes (example)
A classic Uno-like board often has limited SRAM measured in a few kilobytes, larger flash for program space, and about one kilobyte of EEPROM. Plan accordingly.
Using F to save SRAM
Wrap constant text with the flash macro when printing to avoid copying the string into SRAM. This keeps runtime memory lower and more reliable.

screens.title: Memory-Safe Patterns and Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: How to keep your sketch stable on low-RAM boards

narration.text: When working with limited SRAM you must adopt conservative patterns. First, avoid large global arrays unless they are absolutely necessary; if you need a large buffer, consider processing data in smaller chunks. Second, limit or avoid repeated use of dynamic string operations; prefer fixed buffers or incremental writes. Third, store long constant strings in flash using the F macro so they never occupy SRAM. Fourth, initialize min and max variables from real data or sensible sentinels to prevent incorrect comparisons. A common cause of crashes is heap fragmentation created by many short-lived dynamic allocations. The remedy is to minimize allocations and to reuse static buffers. Another subtle pitfall is using too-large local arrays inside functions that consume stack space, which can overlap with dynamic memory on some architectures. Profile your memory usage early: if a sketch works briefly and then fails after some time, heap fragmentation is likely. Always test with representative workloads and watch for Serial prints indicating out-of-memory or failed allocations. A practical rule: when in doubt, prefer static C-style buffers and flash-stored constants on small boards. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Memory-Safe Patterns

Practical Rules to Avoid Memory Problems

Prefer static buffers
Re-use pre-allocated character arrays rather than allocating temporaries. This reduces heap churn and avoids fragmentation.
Use flash for constants
Wrap constant text with the flash macro to keep it out of SRAM during runtime.
Limit local large arrays
Large arrays inside functions consume stack space; prefer globals or smaller chunks to avoid stack/heap collision.
Test with realistic inputs
Run long-duration tests to reveal fragmentation and allocation failures that short tests might hide.

narration.text: These are three compact ideas to keep in mind as you code on small microcontrollers. First, arrays and indexing: arrays group same-typed values and use zero-based indexes; always check bounds to avoid undefined behavior. Second, iterating with loops: a for loop with an index from zero to less-than the array size is the reliable pattern to access all elements without overrun. Third, C-strings versus the Arduino String class: C-strings are memory-efficient and predictable, while the String class is convenient but can fragment SRAM on constrained boards. Hold these principles as you write and test sketches so you choose safe data structures and loop patterns that match your board's memory limits. narration.text: A few final points to carry forward: understand the roles of flash, SRAM, and EEPROM so you store data where it belongs. Use the F macro to print constant strings from flash instead of copying them into SRAM, which preserves precious working memory. Finally, guard against heap fragmentation by minimizing dynamic String usage and reusing static buffers when possible. These combined habits keep sketches running reliably on boards with limited R A M. As you code, test under realistic conditions and watch for failures that appear only after the sketch has run for some time — that is often a memory management signal. With these practices you'll reduce crashes and make your projects easier to scale.
